title: AI Literacy as a Key Driver of User Experience in AI-Powered Assessment: Insights from Socratic Mind
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ AI literacy shapes their experience with an AI-powered assessment tool in higher education. The central problem is that while AI tools are increasingly used in education, students may benefit from them differently depending not just on prior exposure to AI, but on their actual AI literacy. The study asks how AI literacy, usability, and satisfaction relate to student engagement and perceived learning effectiveness when using an AI-based oral assessment system, and whether prior AI exposure or demographic factors matter.

The intervention studied is Socratic Mind, an AI-powered interactive oral assessment tool that uses large language models and automatic speech recognition to conduct spoken Socratic dialogue with learners. Students respond verbally to prompts, receive adaptive follow-up questions, and obtain automated feedback summaries after the interaction. The researchers embedded the tool into course activities as a formative assessment and practice quiz system, then administered surveys measuring user experience, perceived learning effectiveness, engagement, satisfaction, AI literacy, demographics, and prior AI exposure. Analyses included partial least squares structural equation modeling and group comparisons.

The population consisted of 309 valid student respondents at Georgia Institute of Technology, primarily undergraduates in foundational computer science and a junior-level business course, plus a small number of high school dual-enrollment students and one master’s student. The tool was used across a semester in course-related learning activities, with instructors configuring quizzes and question logic. The study context is therefore a single U.S. institution in classroom-linked higher education courses, though the outcome data came from end-of-semester surveys rather than direct performance measures.

The main conclusion is that AI literacy—not prior AI exposure—was the key driver of positive user experience with the tool. Higher AI literacy significantly predicted greater usability, satisfaction, and engagement, and usability and satisfaction strongly predicted perceived learning effectiveness. Students with higher AI literacy rated the system more favorably across all major experience dimensions. The authors argue that AI-powered educational tools should be designed with adaptive guidance, intuitive interfaces, and supports matched to varying literacy levels, and that institutions should build students’ AI literacy explicitly rather than assuming prior exposure is enough.

identified_tools.name: Socratic Mind
identified_tools.description: An interactive AI-powered oral assessment system that uses LLMs and automatic speech recognition to conduct spoken Socratic dialogue, ask adaptive follow-up questions, and provide automated feedback summaries.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a formative assessment practice quiz in undergraduate computer science and business courses across a semester to help students verbalize reasoning, reflect on understanding, and prepare for quizzes and exams.

findings.finding_summary: In a PLS-SEM model with 309 undergraduates, AI literacy significantly predicted perceived usability (β=.301, t=5.093, p<.001), satisfaction (β=.212, t=3.620, p<.001), and engagement (β=.160, t=3.962, p<.001) with Socratic Mind, but did not directly predict perceived learning effectiveness (β=.041, t=0.987, p=.324). Usability and satisfaction were reported as strong direct predictors of perceived learning effectiveness, and the model explained substantial variance in effectiveness (R²=.616) and engagement (R²=.547).
findings.measure: Perceived usability, satisfaction, engagement, and perceived learning effectiveness from UX survey and PLS-SEM path coefficients

findings.finding_summary: Students with higher AI literacy reported significantly more positive perceptions of Socratic Mind than students with lower AI literacy. Group differences were significant for satisfaction (low: M=4.22, SD=0.74, n=143; high: M=4.46, SD=0.67, n=168; t(288.44)=-2.87, p=.004, d=-0.33), usability (t(220.80)=-3.98, p<.001, d=-0.47), effectiveness (t(245.68)=-4.05, p<.001, d=-0.47), and engagement (t(264.34)=-5.83, p<.001, d=-0.68).
findings.measure: Satisfaction, usability, perceived learning effectiveness, and engagement ratings by AI literacy group

findings.finding_summary: Prior AI exposure did not significantly influence students' perceptions of Socratic Mind. Comparisons between low- and high-exposure groups showed no significant differences in satisfaction (t(287.73)=-0.91, p=.362, d=-0.11), usability (t(295.57)=-1.09, p=.278, d=-0.12), effectiveness (t(295.53)=-0.47, p=.636, d=-0.05), or engagement (t(284.50)=-1.12, p=.262, d=-0.13).
findings.measure: Satisfaction, usability, perceived learning effectiveness, and engagement ratings by AI exposure group

findings.finding_summary: Students who had previously used generative AI tools reported slightly higher usability for Socratic Mind than non-users (No: M=4.56, SD=0.64, n=89; Yes: M=4.71, SD=0.48, n=216; t(130.63)=-1.99, p=.048, d=-0.28). However, there were no significant differences for perceived effectiveness (p=.368), engagement (p=.604), satisfaction (p=.457), or overall AI literacy (p=.468).
findings.measure: Usability, effectiveness, engagement, satisfaction, and AI literacy by prior generative AI tool use

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical single-study evaluation with a substantial sample, but it is observational and survey-based rather than an RCT or strong quasi-experimental design. Outcomes are self-reported perceptions and modeled associations, limiting causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports several modest-to-moderate positive effects, including Cohen's d values up to 0.68 for engagement and meaningful path coefficients for usability and satisfaction pathways. However, impacts are largely perceptual rather than direct objective learning outcomes.
